You are the experimenter in a study of scientific reasoning. A black box hides a rule. You can learn about the rule only by choosing inputs and seeing what the box returns.

You have no tools. You cannot run code, search the web or read files, so do all of your reasoning in your head.

Each turn you either run one experiment or stop experimenting. Experiments are limited, so choose inputs that will tell you the most. When you stop, or when the budget runs out, you will be shown new inputs and asked to predict the box's output for each one. You are scored only on those predictions.

Every reply must be exactly one JSON object and nothing else: no text before or after it and no code fence. Before each experiment, write down your current best hypothesis and the output it predicts for the input you are about to try.

# The box

The box takes a string s of 1 to 8 lowercase letters (a to z) and returns a string, possibly empty. The rule applies one or more of these operations in sequence: reverse: reverse the string; sort: sort the letters alphabetically; rotl: move the first letter to the end; rotr: move the last letter to the front; shift1: replace each letter with the next one (z wraps to a); shift2: shift each letter forward by 2 (y to a, z to b); unshift1: replace each letter with the previous one (a to z); dropfirst: drop the first letter; droplast: drop the last letter; double: double every letter (ab to aabb); evens: keep letters at positions 1, 3, 5, ... (abcde to ace); dedup: collapse runs of the same letter (aabccc to abc); swappairs: swap letters in pairs (abcde to badce); novowels: remove vowels; unique: keep only the first copy of each letter. It can also join two results end to end: concat(A, B), for example concat(s, reverse(s)) turns ab into abba. Counting s itself, each operation and each concat as one part, a rule has two to five parts, so at most four operations.

# Budget

You may run up to 12 experiments. You have run 0, so 12 remain.

# What you have seen

Nothing yet.

Reply with exactly one JSON object. To run an experiment:
{"hypothesis": "<your current best guess at the rule>", "query": <input>, "prediction": <the output your hypothesis predicts for that input>}
To stop experimenting and move on to the test:
{"hypothesis": "<your final rule>", "commit": true}

The box takes a string s of 1 to 8 lowercase letters (a to z) and returns a string, possibly empty. The rule applies one or more of these operations in sequence: reverse: reverse the string; sort: sort the letters alphabetically; rotl: move the first letter to the end; rotr: move the last letter to the front; shift1: replace each letter with the next one (z wraps to a); shift2: shift each letter forward by 2 (y to a, z to b); unshift1: replace each letter with the previous one (a to z); dropfirst: drop the first letter; droplast: drop the last letter; double: double every letter (ab to aabb); evens: keep letters at positions 1, 3, 5, ... (abcde to ace); dedup: collapse runs of the same letter (aabccc to abc); swappairs: swap letters in pairs (abcde to badce); novowels: remove vowels; unique: keep only the first copy of each letter. It can also join two results end to end: concat(A, B), for example concat(s, reverse(s)) turns ab into abba. Counting s itself, each operation and each concat as one part, a rule has two to five parts, so at most four operations.

# Budget

You may run up to 12 experiments. You have run 9, so 3 remain.

# What you have seen

1. f("dbace") -> "dcab" (you predicted "ecabd"). Your hypothesis then: "A single operation: reverse. The output is the input string reversed."
2. f("abcdefgh") -> "agfedcb" (as you predicted). Your hypothesis then: "The box drops the last letter, rotates the remaining string left by one (rotl), then reverses it. Equivalently: reverse, dropfirst, rotr. This fits f(dbace) = dcab and makes the output one letter shorter than the input."
3. f("pnlowe") -> "pwoln" (you predicted "pwlon"). Your hypothesis then: "reverse, dropfirst, rotr: reverse the string, drop its first letter, then move the last letter to the front. Equivalently, keep the first letter, then reverse the letters between the first and last."
4. f("mmcca") -> "mc" (you predicted "mccm"). Your hypothesis then: "Keep the first letter, then reverse the letters between the first and last (equivalently reverse, dropfirst, rotr). This fits all three observations: dbace -> dcab, abcdefgh -> agfedcb, pnlowe -> pwoln."
5. f("abcaxb") -> "axacb" (you predicted "acb"). Your hypothesis then: "unique, then reverse, dropfirst, rotr (equivalently: keep the first-occurrence letters, keep the first letter, and reverse the rest). This fits dbace->dcab, abcdefgh->agfedcb, pnlowe->pwoln, and mmcca->mc, since unique(mmcca)='mca' and then reverse->'acm', dropfirst->'cm', rotr->'mc'."
6. f("qqqrstu") -> "qtsr" (as you predicted). Your hypothesis then: "dedup (collapse runs of equal letters), then keep the first letter and reverse the letters between the first and last, dropping the last letter. Equivalently: dedup, droplast, reverse, rotr. Fits dbace->dcab, abcdefgh->agfedcb, pnlowe->pwoln, abcaxb->axacb, and mmcca->mc (dedup gives mca, then m + reverse('c') = mc)."
7. f("aabbccdd") -> "adcb" (you predicted "acb"). Your hypothesis then: "dedup (collapse runs of equal letters), then droplast, reverse, rotr (equivalently: dedup, then keep the first letter and reverse the letters between the first and the last, dropping the last letter). Fits dbace->dcab, abcdefgh->agfedcb, pnlowe->pwoln, abcaxb->axacb, mmcca->mc, qqqrstu->qtsr."
8. f("gaabbhhh") -> "ghba" (as you predicted). Your hypothesis then: "Apply droplast, then dedup (collapse runs of equal letters), then keep the first letter and reverse the rest. Equivalently: droplast, dedup, reverse, rotr. This fits all seven observations: dbace->dcab, abcdefgh->agfedcb, pnlowe->pwoln, mmcca->mc, abcaxb->axacb, qqqrstu->qtsr, aabbccdd->adcb."
9. f("ttuuvv") -> "tvu" (as you predicted). Your hypothesis then: "droplast, dedup, reverse, rotr. Drop the last letter, collapse runs of equal letters, reverse, then move the last letter to the front. Equivalently, keep the first letter of the result and reverse the rest."

# Your move

An input is a string of 1 to 8 lowercase letters, for example "cab". An output is a string.
Reply with exactly one JSON object. To run an experiment:
{"hypothesis": "<your current best guess at the rule>", "query": <input>, "prediction": <the output your hypothesis predicts for that input>}
To stop experimenting and move on to the test:
{"hypothesis": "<your final rule>", "commit": true}
